The definition I have for knowledge;
On the traditional analysis, a person knows a proposition if and only if three conditions hold: the proposition is true, the person believes it, and the person is justified in believing it. Each condition is claimed to be necessary and the three together are claimed to be sufficient. The analysis is traced to Plato and was the textbook default until Gettier's 1963 counterexamples.
It says the proposition is true as separate from someone believing it is true. When it comes to something like god, it is not true, but people say that their belief is the evidence needed. That seems like a settled argument. So there is no knowledge about god just beliefs

Is there knowledge about God, or only belief?

Verdict: It isn’t settled, and the argument as written doesn’t work. It rests on the wrong condition of the definition. There is a stronger argument close by, but it has a well-known counter of its own.

Where your argument breaks

1. It assumes its conclusion.
“God is not true, therefore belief in God isn’t knowledge” only works if non-existence is already established. But that is exactly the point in dispute. A theist can run the mirror image: “God is true, I believe it, therefore it’s knowledge.” Both versions fail for the same reason.

2. The truth condition isn’t a test you can run.
In the traditional analysis, truth is part of what makes something knowledge. It isn’t a procedure for checking a claim, because nobody has a view from outside their own evidence. In practice you only ever assess justification. So using condition 1 as a filter treats your own view as if it settles the question.

3. The symmetry trap.
By the same definition, “God does not exist” counts as knowledge only if it is also justified. An atheist who holds it for bad reasons has, at best, a lucky true belief.

4. Scope creep.
“No knowledge about God” is too broad. You can know things about the concept (Anselm’s definition, for example) or about what believers hold. What you mean is narrower: there is no knowledge that God exists.

The repair (your job, not mine)

The attack on “my belief is my evidence” belongs in a different condition. You can probably see which one.

Build the argument yourself. Test: the repaired version must still go through even if you assume God exists. If it does, you’ve stopped begging the question.

Why the repaired version still isn’t settled

Expect these objections when you pressure-test it:

Most theists don’t say “belief is the evidence.” That’s the folk version. Philosophers of religion appeal to arguments, testimony and religious experience. Attacking the folk version is attacking a straw man.
Plantinga’s reformed epistemology. He argues belief in God can be properly basic: warranted without inferential evidence, in the same way as belief in other minds or in the reliability of your memory.
Plantinga’s sharpest move (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000). He argues you can’t settle whether theistic belief is justified without first settling whether it is true. On externalist accounts, justification depends on whether the belief-forming process is reliable. That in turn depends on whether God exists. If he’s right, your repaired argument collapses back into the original problem.
Clifford vs James. Clifford (1877) held it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. James (1896) argued that some live, forced choices permit belief beyond the evidence. Neither side has decisively won.
A tension in your own vault

Your Zettelkasten is Popperian, and Popper rejected justificationism outright. For him, knowledge is conjecture that has survived criticism, not justified true belief.

Under Popper the question changes. It is no longer “is belief in God justified?” but “is the God hypothesis open to criticism or refutation?” That arguably fits your system better than the traditional definition does. If the JTB note is in the vault as a historical reference point, that’s fine. If it’s meant as your working definition, it conflicts with the rest of the vault.

Uncertainty
What wouldn’t change my view: that the original argument assumes its conclusion. That is a structural flaw, not a matter of opinion.
What would change my view of the repaired version: if you hold an internalist view of justification (justification depends on reasons you can access), the repair is strong. If you hold an externalist one, Plantinga’s objection bites hard.
Next action

In a fleeting note, write one sentence restating your argument using only the justification condition, phrased so it still works if God exists.

Does the same thing carry for ghosts and fairies? So i can't claim to know that ghosts don't exist? So all possibilities that can me imagined I can at most belief don't exist but never know?

Ghosts, fairies, and knowing that something doesn’t exist

Verdict: No. You’ve overcorrected. My earlier point wasn’t that you can’t know something doesn’t exist. It was that you can’t get there by assuming it isn’t true. You can know ghosts don’t exist in the same way you know most things: fallibly, with good justification.

The mistake: treating knowledge as certainty
The traditional definition needs justification, not proof.
If knowledge required ruling out every imaginable possibility, you couldn’t know your car is where you parked it. A thief, a tow truck or a simulation glitch are all imaginable.
That position exists: it’s radical scepticism. It’s internally consistent, but it doesn’t single out ghosts. It abolishes almost all empirical knowledge.
The mainstream view is fallibilism: you can know something while accepting you might be wrong and would revise if new evidence turned up.
How you know a negative

“You can’t prove a negative” is a myth. You know there’s no elephant in your fridge.

The test is: if X existed, what would I expect to observe? Absence of evidence counts as evidence of absence, in proportion to how much evidence you’d expect to find if X were real.

Ghosts are claimed to be seen, heard, and to move objects. That means they should be detectable. Yet:

centuries of looking, including controlled investigations, have produced nothing robust;
well-understood alternatives explain the reports: sleep paralysis, infrasound, carbon monoxide, pareidolia and suggestion;
they’d break well-corroborated physics. Something that reflects light, so it can be seen, but passes through walls is a contradiction, not just an oddity.

Fairies: the best-known evidence, the Cottingley photographs, was admitted to be faked.

So “ghosts don’t exist” can be justified, believed and (very probably) true. That counts as knowledge, held open to revision.

Where your worry does have teeth

Some hypotheses are built to be undetectable. Sagan’s example is a dragon in the garage that is invisible, incorporeal, gives off no heat and floats. Every possible test has been ruled out in advance.

You can’t collect expected-but-missing evidence against something like that. But the claim also tells you nothing, because nothing would be different if it were false. The honest response isn’t “I believe it doesn’t exist”. It’s “there’s nothing here to assess”, so you withhold belief.

This is why God and ghosts aren’t automatically the same case. It depends on which concept of God:

A God who intervenes (answers prayers, heals, acts in history) makes predictions, so the expected-evidence test applies.
A deist God who never acts sits much closer to the dragon.
The same point in Popperian terms

For Popper, everything is conjecture, including “electrons exist”. So the meaningful line isn’t know versus believe. It’s:

Status    Example
Well-corroborated    “Ghosts don’t exist” (the claim that they do has repeatedly failed tests)
Untested    A new, unexamined claim
Untestable    The garage dragon

Lacking certainty is universal. It isn’t a special weakness of negative claims.

Uncertainty
Fallibilism is the majority view, not unanimous. If you side with the infallibilists, your conclusion follows, but for everything, not just ghosts and fairies.
The ghost case leans on inference to the best explanation. If you reject that form of reasoning, the case for knowing ghosts don’t exist gets weaker.
Next action

Pick one concept of God, either interventionist or deist, and write one line in a fleeting note: “If this God existed, I’d expect to observe ___.” Whether you can fill the blank tells you which category it falls into.

Wesley Salmon’s criticism of Popper

Verdict: Salmon’s 1981 paper “Rational Prediction” argues that Popper’s rejection of induction makes rational theory-based prediction impossible. Popper can tell you which theories have been refuted. He can’t tell you, without sneaking induction back in, why you should rely on any surviving theory to predict what happens next. 
utu

The argument, step by step
Popper’s position. Evidence can only refute theories, never establish them. His concept of corroboration measures how well a conjecture has stood up to severe criticism and testing. That’s a record of the past. Even on Popper’s own account, you can’t infer from a theory’s corroboration that what it says about the future will be true. 
conjecturesandrefutations
utu
Prediction needs a choice. To act, say to build a bridge, you have to pick one theory from the many that haven’t been refuted. Salmon notes that if there were no rational basis for choosing among the unrefuted alternatives, Popper would presumably agree there’d be no such thing as rational prediction. 
conjecturesandrefutations
Popper’s answer is to use the best-corroborated theory. Salmon’s reply is that he can’t see how it’s rational to judge theories for prediction by a criterion that is explicitly claimed to have no predictive import. 
utu
The dilemma. Either corroboration does tell you something about the future, in which case it’s induction in disguise. Or it doesn’t, in which case choosing the best-tested theory for prediction has no rational basis.

His closing line put it memorably: you might manage to cut every inductive element out of science, but the patient, stripped of its predictive power, would die. 
utu

A concrete version

Take two theories that have passed every test so far:

T1: steel behaves as the engineering textbooks say.
T2: identical to T1, except that bridges built after 2027 collapse.

Every test ever run happened before 2027, so both theories passed all of them equally. Why build on T1? “Because it’s been tested” doesn’t separate them. You seem to need the assumption that the future will resemble the past, and that assumption is induction.

Popperian replies
Popper’s own reply: preferring the best-tested theory is a rational critical preference. It’s the one that has survived criticism, with no claim that it’s more probably true.
Later defenders: some argue that critical rationalism does specify which predictions are rational: those made in ways that have so far withstood criticism and that would be easy to criticise if they went wrong. Demanding more justification than that restarts the regress from your last question. 
criticalrationalism
David Deutsch, the line your vault follows: we reject T2 not because of past track record but because it’s a bad explanation. Nothing explains why 2027 should matter, and the date could be changed to anything without loss. Good explanations are hard to vary.
Not everyone is persuaded. One paper calls Salmon’s problem the Achilles heel of Popper’s critical method, and argues that both Popper’s and Alan Musgrave’s responses fail. 
philarchive
Why this matters for you
Your God position. It now rests on “has survived the criticisms I know of”. Salmon’s question applies directly: why should surviving criticism count in a belief’s favour?
Your last question about justification. Every Popperian reply here is a way of stopping that regress by a provisional decision, Popper’s piles in the swamp, rather than reaching bedrock.
Uncertainty
Genuinely open. Philosophers of science still disagree on whether Salmon wins.
My tentative view: Deutsch’s reply is the strongest, but it may only relocate the problem. Why expect hard-to-vary explanations to keep holding tomorrow? That looks like a bet that the world is regular, which is close to what induction assumes.
What would change my view: a defence of “rely on the best-tested theory” that makes no assumption at all about the future resembling the past.
Next action

Write one sentence explaining why you’d trust the bridge built on T1, without using any premise about the future resembling the past.

You said "My belief that no God of kind X exists has survived every criticism I know of, and here is what would refute it." I am unconvinced by the survived every criticism. I have seen religious people agree with criticisms so the only difference is I think the belief survives the criticism not that it did

Is “survived criticism” just a judgement?

Verdict: You’re right about the wording, and it’s a good catch. “Survived” is always someone’s judgement, and the theist makes the same judgement about their own belief. But the real difference isn’t who judges. It’s whether the belief could have lost, and other people can check that.

Where you’re right
“Has survived every criticism I know of” really means “I judge it has survived”. My template overstated it.
In that form, it’s symmetrical with the believer who hears a criticism, agrees it’s a fair point, and keeps believing.
Surviving a test versus never being at risk
A test only counts if it could have failed. Popper called this the severity of a test. A belief that couldn’t have lost hasn’t survived anything; it was never in the fight.
Agreeing with a criticism while leaving the belief untouched means the criticism never landed. For example: “Yes, suffering is a real problem for my faith. God works in mysterious ways.” The belief was protected, not tested. Popper called these moves conventionalist stratagems: rescuing a theory by adjusting it so that no evidence can count against it.
The line isn’t atheist versus theist. Some theist philosophers, such as Richard Swinburne, build probabilistic cases where evidence can genuinely count for or against God. Some atheists hold their view dogmatically. The real line is exposed beliefs versus protected ones.
Who judges: not you alone

For Popper, objectivity isn’t a property of one person’s mind. It lies in claims being testable by others. The markers are visible from outside:

Marker    Exposed belief    Protected belief
What would refute it is stated in advance    Yes    No, or shifts after the fact
Standards are fixed before testing    Yes    Adjusted when a test goes badly
The same standard is applied to rival views    Yes    Rivals held to a stricter bar
There’s a record of actually revising it    Yes    Criticism “accepted”, nothing changes

You don’t have to trust your own judgement that the belief survived. You let others check whether it was ever at risk.

The uncomfortable part: your own belief

By this standard, your atheism hasn’t survived anything yet. The scope and falsifier fields on its claim card are still blank. Right now it sits where you’ve put the believer: convinced, and judging its own survival.

That isn’t a failing; it’s just the current state of the card. It’s also exactly what your claim-card format is built to fix.

Revised template

I believe no God of kind X exists. It would be refuted by Y, stated in advance. So far, Y hasn’t happened.

This drops “survived” altogether. It replaces a judgement call with a test anyone can check.

Uncertainty
Severity is also a judgement, so the regress returns at a finer grain. The difference is that it becomes a judgement others can inspect, not a private conviction.
Salmon’s question still stands: why should Y not happening count in the belief’s favour? I haven’t answered that, and neither has anyone conclusively.
Next action

Complete one sentence: “My belief that no God of kind X exists would be refuted if ___.”
